introduction:
Carrots and parsnips share several root pests and diseases. Carrots are especially vulnerable to carrot fly; parsnips also suffer from old seed and canker.

Start with fresh seed, deep well-prepared soil and a clean seedbed. Avoid fresh manure; use resistant varieties where available.

copy.recognise: Old seed, cold or dry soil and deep sowing can all delay or prevent emergence. Check conditions before resowing.
copy.act: Sow again with fresh seed if the season still allows.
copy.prevent: Use fresh seed each year. Keep the drill moist until seedlings emerge; a few radish seeds can mark the row.

copy.recognise: Sunlight turns exposed carrot crowns green. Unlike green potatoes, green carrots are not harmful, but look unsightly.
copy.prevent: Earth up around exposed crowns during the growing season.

copy.recognise: Rust-coloured crown damage may resemble staining or canker; the precise cause needs confirmation.
copy.act: Lift and discard badly affected roots.
copy.prevent: Improve drainage, avoid root injury and seek a diagnosis before choosing a long crop break.

copy.recognise: Carrot surface damage associated with clay; check for pests or rot. The cause is uncertain.
copy.act: Inspect affected roots; seek identification for recurring damage. Discard active decay.
copy.prevent: Prepare well-drained, workable soil; use a raised bed where necessary.

copy.recognise: Leaves turn reddish, then yellow. Maggots tunnel in carrots or damage parsnip surfaces. Seedlings may die; roots may rot.
copy.act: No cure. Minor surface damage on large parsnips may be trimmed away.
copy.prevent: Cover completely with insect-proof mesh on rotated ground. Sow thinly. Carrots sown after mid-May or lifted before late August may avoid peak attacks.

copy.recognise: Roots fork when tips meet stones, compaction or injury. Fresh manure and uneven seedbeds can contribute.
copy.act: There is no treatment for an already forked root.
copy.prevent: Prepare workable soil, remove larger stones and avoid compaction or fresh manure before sowing.

copy.recognise: Crowding, drought, poor soil or pest damage can keep roots small. First check variety and maturity.
copy.act: Check spacing, water and root health. Thin carefully and correct confirmed poor fertility.
copy.prevent: Prepare workable soil in advance; maintain suitable spacing and steady moisture.

copy.recognise: Roots split after heavy rain or watering follows a dry spell. Leaving mature roots in wet autumn soil also increases the risk.
copy.act: There is no cure. Use split roots immediately; they will not store.
copy.prevent: Water regularly and deeply in drought. Mulch with compost to steady moisture. Where splitting recurs, lift maincrop carrots before prolonged wet weather.

copy.recognise: Soft root or crown rot develops white cottony mould, sometimes with black resting bodies. Both growing crops and stored roots can be affected.
copy.act: Remove infected plants and rotten stored roots promptly; keep them out of home compost.
copy.prevent: Store sound roots and check regularly. Clear infected debris, improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil.

copy.recognise: Greenfly cause distorted, discoloured, stunted leaves, especially in warm, dry summers. They can also transmit motley dwarf virus.
copy.act: Tolerate small colonies; squash damaging colonies and encourage natural predators.
copy.prevent: Inspect young crops and maintain steady growth. Aphid management cannot guarantee protection from viruses.

copy.recognise: Large black patches develop on stored carrots, often with no obvious symptoms before harvest.
copy.act: Remove and destroy diseased roots promptly.
copy.prevent: Store only sound roots in a cool, ventilated place and inspect regularly. Do not grow carrots on the same land next year. Avoid reusing a problem storage site year after year.

copy.recognise: Yellow mottling, red outer leaves and stunting may indicate carrot motley dwarf, an aphid-transmitted virus complex.
copy.act: Confirm the cause and remove badly affected plants; infected plants cannot be cured.
copy.prevent: Inspect young growth, encourage aphid predators and remove damaging colonies. Virus spread can still occur.

introduction: Check alliums at the leaf base as well as above ground. Feeding damage, rot and growth checks can look alike. Use sound bulbs with thick necks or splits promptly; store only dry, healthy bulbs. White rot needs particular care to avoid spreading soil.

copy.recognise: A premature flower stalk forms, often after cold or checked growth. Oversized sets can be more susceptible.
copy.act: Pinch out small flower stems without loosening bulbs; use affected bulbs early.
copy.prevent: Choose suitable small or heat-treated sets, plant at the recommended season and avoid growth checks.

copy.recognise: Bulbs split at the base, often after heavy rain or watering follows prolonged drought.
copy.act: Use sound split bulbs promptly; they will not store well.
copy.prevent: Keep growth steady with watering during dry summer spells.

copy.recognise: Onion sets may form twin bulbs; large sets and growth checks can contribute. Shallots naturally form clusters.
copy.prevent: Use suitable onion sets, plant in season and maintain steady growth. Shallot division is normal.

pages.name: Birds Pulling Sets
pages.symptom: Newly planted onion sets are pulled out of the soil just as they begin to grow.

copy.recognise: Newly planted onion sets are pulled out before they establish. Birds may investigate their exposed dry tips.
copy.act: Replant sound lifted sets promptly before their roots dry out.
copy.prevent: Firm sets at normal depth and guard with secure netting until rooted. Check for trapped wildlife.

pages.name: Onion Fly
pages.symptom: Tunnelled bulbs with 1/4 in. white maggots.

copy.recognise: Yellow, drooping leaves accompany maggots feeding at bulb bases. Seedlings may die; older plants fail to develop.
copy.act: Remove badly affected plants and infested bulbs.
copy.prevent: Use insect-proof mesh with rotation. Clear crop debris; sets are less vulnerable than seedlings.

copy.recognise: Dark-green leaves may flop after excessive nitrogen. But drooping alone also needs checks for watering problems, pests or normal maturity.
copy.act: Check roots and bulb bases before assuming a feeding problem.
copy.prevent: Avoid fresh manure and excessive nitrogen; do not add fertiliser blindly.

copy.recognise: Swollen, distorted leaves accompany soft bulbs. Microscopic stem and bulb nematodes may kill young plants.
copy.act: Remove affected plants and seek a confirmed diagnosis.
copy.prevent: Avoid moving infested soil. Plan a suitable rotation for the identified nematode and its host range.

copy.recognise: Black spots and blotches develop on leaves or bulbs of young plants; leaves thicken and twist. Leeks are particularly vulnerable.
copy.act: Remove affected plants and seek confirmation.
copy.prevent: Avoid moving affected soil and seek advice on a long crop break; the fungus can persist for years.

copy.recognise: Orange pustules mark leek and garlic leaves. Often cosmetic, heavy attacks yellow foliage and check growth.
copy.act: Remove badly affected leaves and keep plants growing steadily.
copy.prevent: Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; water roots in dry spells and clear infected debris.

copy.recognise: Onions retain unusually thick, fleshy necks and store poorly. Excess nitrogen or deep sowing may contribute.
copy.act: Use sound affected bulbs early; do not store them with well-ripened bulbs.
copy.prevent: Avoid overfeeding and deep sowing. Additional feed will not cure a thick neck.

copy.recognise: Leek tips turn white and papery in autumn; damage spreads down leaves and may stunt growth.
copy.act: Remove badly diseased plants and affected debris.
copy.prevent: Avoid an affected bed the following season; improve drainage and avoid prolonged leaf wetness.

copy.recognise: Grey mould develops on onion leaves after wet weather, sometimes followed by black sootiness. Growth and storage quality suffer.
copy.act: Remove badly affected material. Dry harvested bulbs thoroughly and keep suspect bulbs out of long storage.
copy.prevent: Rotate, space well and improve drainage. Avoid nearby overwintered infected onions; choose resistant varieties.
